'''Aise Johan de Jong''' (born 30 January 1966)<ref name=r1/> is a Dutch mathematician and professor of mathematics at [[Columbia University]]. His research interests include [[arithmetic geometry]] and [[algebraic geometry]]. He maintains the [[Stacks Project]].

==Early life and education==
De Jong was born in [[Bruges]], Belgium on 30 January 1966.<ref name=r1/> He attended the [[Christelijk Gymnasium Sorghvliet]] in [[The Hague]], Netherlands.<ref name=r1/> He obtained his master's degree at [[Leiden University]] in 1987, under the supervision of Antonius Van de Ven.<ref name=r1/> He earned his Ph.D. ''cum laude'' at the [[Radboud University Nijmegen]] in 1992, under the supervision of [[Frans Oort]] and [[Joseph H. M. Steenbrink]].<ref name=r1/><ref>{{MathGenealogy |id=7647 }}</ref>

==Career==
De Jong spent 1 year as a visitor at the [[Max Planck Institute for Mathematics]], 3 months as a visitor at [[Bielefeld University]], and then 3 years as a fellow at the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]] stationed at [[Utrecht University]].<ref name=r1/><ref name="Steele"/> He was a Benjamin Peirce Assistant Professor at [[Harvard University]] from 1995 to 1996.<ref name="Steele"/> He was a professor of mathematics at [[Princeton University]] from 1996 to 1998 and then worked at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] from 1998 to 2005.<ref name="Steele"/> He moved to [[Columbia University]] as a professor of mathematics in 2005.<ref name="Steele"/>

==Work==
In 1996, de Jong developed his theory of [[Resolution of singularities#De Jong.27s method|alterations]] which was used by [[Fedor Bogomolov]] and Tony Pantev (1996) and [[Dan Abramovich]] and de Jong (1997) to prove [[resolution of singularities]] in [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] 0 and to prove a weaker result for varieties of all dimensions in characteristic ''p'' which is strong enough to act as a substitute for resolution for many purposes.<ref>{{citation|last=de Jong|first= A. J. |url=https://www.numdam.org/item?id=PMIHES_1996__83__51_0 |title=Smoothness, semi-stability and alterations|journal= Inst. Hautes Études Sci. Publ. Math.|volume= 83 |year=1996|pages= 51–93|doi=10.1007/BF02698644|s2cid= 53581802 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last1=Bogomolov|first1= Fedor A.|last2=Pantev|first2=Tony G. |arxiv=alg-geom/9603019|title=Weak Hironaka theorem|journal= Mathematical Research Letters|volume= 3 |year=1996|issue=3|pages= 299–307|doi=10.4310/mrl.1996.v3.n3.a1|bibcode= 1996alg.geom..3019B|s2cid= 14010069}}</ref><ref>{{Citation | last1=Abramovich | first1=D | last2=de Jong | first2=A. J. | title=Smoothness, semistability, and toroidal geometry | arxiv=alg-geom/9603018 | mr=1487237 | year=1997 | journal=Journal of Algebraic Geometry   | volume=6 | issue=4 | pages=789–801| bibcode=1996alg.geom..3018A }}</ref>

In 2005, de Jong started the [[Stacks Project]], "an open source textbook and reference work on [[algebraic stack]]s and the [[algebraic geometry]] needed to define them."<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Stacks Project » About|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/about|publisher=[[Columbia University|columbia.edu]]|accessdate=30 August 2013}}</ref> The book that the project has generated currently runs to more than 7500 pages as of July 2022.<ref>{{Cite book|author=Johan de Jong|title=The Stacks Project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/download/book.pdf|accessdate=29 January 2017|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
In 1998 he was an Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Berlin.<ref>{{cite book|author=de Jong, A. J.|chapter=Barsotti-Tate groups and crystals|title=Doc. Math. (Bielefeld) Extra Vol. ICM Berlin, 1998, vol. II|year=1998|pages=259–265|chapter-url=https://www.elibm.org/ft/10011661000}}</ref> He won the [[Cole Prize]] in 2000 for his theory of alterations.<ref name="r1">{{Cite journal |year=2000 |title=2000 Cole Prize |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200004/comm-cole.pdf |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=481–482}}</ref> In the same year, De Jong became a correspondent of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/correspondents/5114 |title=Aise de Jong |publisher=Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences |accessdate=4 August 2015 |archive-date=14 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181014010136/https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/correspondents/5114 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2022 he received the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize|Leroy P. Steele Prize for Mathematical Exposition]].<ref name="Steele">{{cite web |url=http://www.ams.org/news?news_id=6894 |title=Aise Johan de Jong receives 2022 Steele Prize for Mathematical Exposition |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |date=9 December 2021 |access-date=7 March 2024}}</ref>

==Personal life==
De Jong lives in New York City with his wife, [[Cathy O'Neil]], and their three sons.<ref name=mathbabeAbout>{{cite web|url=https://mathbabe.org/about/|accessdate=25 July 2013|title=mathbabe.org about page|date=11 June 2011 }}</ref>
